name: MDMA

binding.tissue_or_cell: HEK293 stably expressing human SERT, release of preloaded [3H]-5-HT
binding.notes: Simmler et al 2013, human transporter. Note that rat synaptosome assays (Baumann/Rothman) give SERT release EC50 ~75 nM — 70× more potent. The species difference is real and matters.
Rat synaptosome: 154 nM (much more potent at rat DAT).
MDMA is most potent at NET — explains the sympathomimetic profile.
Weak partial agonist. Functional data: 5-HT2A activation contributes little at clinical doses.
Setola & Roth 2003. 5-HT2B agonism is the proposed mechanism of MDMA-associated valvular heart disease (fenfluramine-like). Active metabolite MDA is more potent at 5-HT2B (Ki ~100 nM).
Human TAAR1 affinity is much weaker for amphetamines; rat data is not a good predictor.
Baumann 2012 Table 1 — rat brain synaptosomes, [3H]5-HT release, 1 µM reserpine, selective blockers isolating one transporter per arm. Same-table companion to the DAT and NET values.
Baumann 2012 Table 1 — [3H]MPP+ release. The paper's own DAT/SERT ratio (0.97) is arithmetically consistent with these cells.

Baumann 2012 Table 1 — [3H]MPP+ release. On this assay MDMA is non-selective across all three transporters; three human studies on other bases put DAT well behind, so basis and species must be shown wherever this is plotted.

functional.notes: Racemic and S-MDMA show weak partial agonism; R-MDMA has negligible functional activity despite higher binding affinity. Stereoselective dissociation between binding and function.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: MDMA is primarily a transporter substrate, not a GPCR agonist of significance. It enters cells via DAT/NET/SERT, then triggers reverse transport (efflux) of monoamines through the same transporters. Inside the neuron, it also disrupts VMAT2 vesicular storage. The 5-HT release dominates the SSC subjective profile; concurrent NE release drives cardiovascular effects; weak DA release (low at human DAT) contributes to reinforcement. The mechanism-based inhibition of CYP2D6 — via reactive quinone/quinone-methide intermediates from the catechol metabolite HHMA — irreversibly inactivates the enzyme that clears MDMA itself, producing the well-documented nonlinear PK.

neuroimaging.finding: MDMA attenuates left amygdala response to angry faces at 1.5 mg/kg PO (no effect on fearful faces) and enhances ventral striatum response to happy faces at 0.75 mg/kg PO
Chronic ecstasy users show reduced SERT availability throughout cerebral cortex (-19 to -46%) and hippocampus (-21%), with striking sparing of the SERT-rich striatum.

metabolism.notes: Primary O-demethylenation pathway. CYP2D6 catalyses the demethylenation that generates the catechol HHMA, which then forms reactive ortho-quinones that covalently bind and inactivate CYP2D6 — this is the mechanism-based inhibition.
Primary N-demethylation enzyme — produces active metabolite MDA. CYP2B6 contributes more than CYP2D6 to this pathway.
Methylates HHMA. HMMA is the major urinary metabolite.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: CYP2D6 inhibition (paroxetine inhibits, MDMA is a 2D6 substrate)
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Paroxetine pretreatment increases MDMA AUC by ~30% but blunts subjective effects via SSRI block of SERT — net effect is reduced euphoria with higher exposure.
Massive AUC increase reported in case reports; fatalities documented in HIV patients combining MDMA with protease inhibitors.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: SERT block (5-HT reuptake blockade competing with MDMA at the transporter)
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Blunts MDMA subjective effects (SERT competition); risk of serotonin syndrome at high combined doses.
Severe risk: massive 5-HT accumulation → serotonin syndrome, hyperthermia, fatality. Absolute contraindication.
drug_interactions_pk.notes: Citation removed: this value was attributed to pmid:10605976, which is H. pylori faecal/oral shedding. Verified against PubMed/Crossref in the 2026-08-01 topicality audit. The number is retained but is now unsourced — treat as unverified.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PM status modestly increases MDMA exposure (~30% higher Cmax) and prolongs half-life, but the effect is much smaller than expected because MDMA itself rapidly inhibits CYP2D6 — within 1 h of a 100 mg dose, even EMs are functionally phenoconverted to PM status. The auto-inhibition takes ~10 days to resolve (slow CYP2D6 resynthesis). Practical implication: re-dosing within a week stacks exposure unpredictably regardless of genotype. COMT Val/Met polymorphism affects HMMA formation kinetics. 5-HTTLPR short/short carriers report stronger subjective effects.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Acute pharmacodynamic tachyphylaxis within hours of redosing: in a controlled human trial (n=10), a second 100 mg dose 4 h later produced effects similar to a single dose despite doubling MDMA plasma concentrations.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: No physical withdrawal syndrome. Post-acute 'comedown' (24-72 h) — dysphoria, fatigue, irritability, occasional depressive episodes — reflects depleted 5-HT stores rather than receptor adaptation. Resolves spontaneously; not pathognomonic of dependence.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Cardiac valvular fibrosis with chronic/repeated heavy use (fenfluramine-like mechanism). Epidemiological evidence supports increased VHD risk in regular MDMA users.

Weak hERG block at supratherapeutic concentrations; clinically relevant QT prolongation usually requires overdose or co-ingestion. Hyperthermia from MDMA toxicity is the dominant cardiac concern, not QT.
MDMA rapidly decreases vesicular monoamine (VMAT-2) transport in rat striatum after high-dose administration; unlike methamphetamine, the deficit partially recovers within 24 h.

Inactivates the enzyme that makes serotonin — by oxidising its sulfhydryl groups, not by binding it, and partly driven by the dopamine MDMA itself releases. Rodent activity falls 30–60% within 1–3 h; a low dose recovers within 24 h without new protein synthesis, while past ~3 days after a high dose the enzyme no longer reactivates. This is the mechanism behind the days-after flatness. Human evidence is a single autopsied heavy polydrug user with no dose history, so the magnitude in people is unestablished.

demographic_differences.sex: Women show ~30-40% higher Cmax and stronger subjective effects per mg/kg, partly explained by lower body water and lower lean body mass. Women also have higher risk of MDMA-associated hyponatremia (combination of SIADH + polydipsia + smaller TBW).
demographic_differences.weight: Fixed-dose protocols (e.g., 125 mg flat) produce wide exposure range — light users get effective ~2 mg/kg, heavy users get ~1 mg/kg. Weight-adjusted dosing is preferred clinically.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment markedly extends half-life (CYP2D6 inhibition + reduced phase II capacity).

data_gaps_remaining: Exact human 5-HT2B Ki (Setola data sometimes cited as 500 nM, sometimes as higher)
notes: MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD: MAPS/Lykos submitted NDA Dec 2023 based on MAPP1 (NCT03537014, n=90) and MAPP2 (n=104) Phase 3 trials, both meeting primary endpoint (CAPS-5 reduction vs placebo+therapy). FDA issued Complete Response Letter Aug 2024 citing functional unblinding, AE underreporting, and concerns about therapy delivery — not efficacy. Drug listed in DEA Schedule I; FDA breakthrough designation 2017. The Holze 2024 enantiomer trial (NCT05277636) showed S-MDMA 100 mg ≈ racemic 125 mg ≈ R-MDMA 300 mg for overall effect intensity.

name: MDA

binding.notes: MDA induces release of 5-HT, DA, and NE. Slightly serotonin-selective vs DA but less so than MDMA (DAT:SERT ratio ≈ 0.36, less SERT-selective than MDMA).

MDA has substantially greater direct 5-HT2A agonist activity than MDMA — this explains its more psychedelic, less prosocial subjective profile. Particularly the (R)-(−)-MDA isomer is more 5-HT2A-active.
5× more potent at 5-HT2B than MDMA. MDA is the major active metabolite of MDMA — chronic MDMA users get repeated 5-HT2B exposure via MDA, driving VHD risk.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Mixed entactogen-psychedelic. Like MDMA, drives transporter-mediated monoamine efflux, but with substantially greater direct postsynaptic 5-HT2A agonism, producing visual/perceptual effects MDMA lacks.

routes.subject_demographics: 12 women, 11 men; healthy adults; equimolar to 100 mg MDMA
routes.notes: Holze 2025 — MDA produces qualitatively more psychedelic (5D-ASC) effects than MDMA at equimolar doses; comparable cardiovascular effects.

metabolism.notes: O-demethylenation. MDA, like MDMA, is also a mechanism-based inhibitor of CYP2D6.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Contraindicated — serotonin syndrome risk identical to MDMA.
drug_interactions_pk.notes: Citation removed: this value was attributed to pmid:10605976, which is H. pylori faecal/oral shedding. Verified against PubMed/Crossref in the 2026-08-01 topicality audit. The number is retained but is now unsourced — treat as unverified.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Same auto-inhibition pattern as MDMA; CYP2D6 PM status has limited PK impact due to substrate-induced enzyme inactivation.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Same as MDMA — depletion of presynaptic 5-HT pools, transient SERT downregulation.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: No physical withdrawal; post-acute serotonergic comedown.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Cardiac valvulopathy risk; MDA is the more potent 5-HT2B agonist of the MDxx family.

data_gaps_remaining: Detailed human transporter EC50 (Simmler did not include MDA; rat synaptosome data dominates the literature)
notes: MDA is both a recreational drug and the active N-demethyl metabolite of MDMA. Its longer half-life (~8 h) explains the persistent next-day stimulant tail after MDMA use. Schedule I.

name: MDE

binding.notes: Full SERT releaser like MDMA.
EC50 > 100,000 nM — does NOT release dopamine appreciably. This is the key distinction from MDMA. Rat synaptosome data: dopamine release EC50 = 622 nM, Emax 61% (partial releaser).
Weaker 5-HT2A than MDMA.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Selective 5-HT/NE release with minimal DA release — pure entactogen profile, less euphoric/stimulant than MDMA. Lower abuse liability hypothesised but not proven clinically.

routes.notes: Half-life ~4 h (shorter than MDMA). Tmax ~2 h.

metabolism.notes: N-deethylation yields MDA. O-demethylenation analogous to MDMA.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Same serotonin syndrome risk as MDMA.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Less mechanism-based inhibition than MDMA; CYP2D6 PMs may show more pronounced exposure changes.

notes: N-ethyl substitution markedly reduces DA-releasing activity vs MDMA — explains the colder, less reinforcing, more 'pure empathogen' subjective profile users report. Was briefly used in early MDMA-assisted psychotherapy when MDMA was scheduled.

name: Mdea

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Duplicate of MDE — see MDE record for full data.

notes: DUPLICATE: This entry is the same compound as 'MDE' in the same list. Recommend deduplication. See MDE record.

name: S-(+)-MDMA

binding.notes: S-MDMA is the more potent monoamine releaser of the two enantiomers — particularly at DAT and NET. Drives the stimulant component of racemic MDMA.
Weak partial agonist (functionally weak despite measurable binding).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: The 'stimulant enantiomer' — more potent DA release, more oxytocin release, shorter half-life. Drives the euphoric, energizing component of racemic MDMA.

routes.notes: Holze/Liechti 2024. S-MDMA half-life only ~4.1 h vs R-MDMA ~12 h — S-enantiomer is preferentially cleared (probably faster CYP2D6 metabolism). Subjective effects strongly favour stimulation/'drug high'/happiness; greater SBP/DBP increase than R-MDMA.

data_gaps_remaining: S-MDMA specific transporter EC50 at human transporters
notes: S-(+)-MDMA is the more stimulant-like enantiomer; 100 mg S-MDMA ≈ 125 mg racemic MDMA in overall acute effect intensity. Not currently in clinical development as a standalone agent — the racemic mixture (midomafetamine) is what Lykos submitted. Category 'Antidepressant' in source is misleading; this is the same class as MDMA.

name: R-(-)-MDMA

binding.notes: Higher specific 5-HT2A binding affinity than S-MDMA but NEGLIGIBLE functional activity — a binding/function dissociation. So 'psychedelic-like' marketing claims need scepticism — in humans, R-MDMA did NOT produce more psychedelic effects than S-MDMA at the doses tested.
Retains SERT-releasing activity (less than S-enantiomer).
Much less DA release than S-MDMA — proposed safety advantage (less reinforcing, less hyperthermic, less neurotoxic in animals).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Preferential SERT-driven 5-HT release with minimal DA release. Animal data: lower locomotor stimulation, lower neurotoxicity signal, lower hyperthermia. Hypothesised as a 'safer' therapeutic enantiomer but the 2024 human trial showed comparable subjective intensity at equipotent doses (300 mg R ≈ 125 mg racemic).

routes.notes: R-MDMA half-life ~12 h (3× longer than S). Slower CYP2D6 metabolism.
Dose-doubled R-MDMA — exposure roughly doubles linearly (less nonlinear than racemic).

data_gaps_remaining: Whether R-MDMA's preclinical safety advantages survive at therapeutically equivalent doses
notes: R-(−)-MDMA is being explored as a potentially safer therapeutic alternative to racemic MDMA. MindMed and others have programs. The human data (Holze 2024) tempers preclinical enthusiasm — at equipotent doses (~300 mg R ≈ 125 mg racemic), overall subjective intensity, MEQ30, and 5D-ASC are similar; the hoped-for 'more psychedelic, less stimulant' dissociation did not emerge in humans.

name: Lys-MDA

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Lysine-amide prodrug of MDA. The parent molecule has no intrinsic monoamine activity; hydrolytic cleavage by aminopeptidases / esterases releases MDA gradually, producing a flatter, delayed exposure curve. Same downstream pharmacology as MDA once liberated.

routes.subject_demographics: 12 women, 11 men; healthy adults; equimolar to 92 mg MDA
routes.notes: Holze 2025. Lys-MDA produced MDA-like subjective effects with markedly delayed onset and lower peak intensity — confirms prodrug behaviour. Tmax of liberated MDA delayed vs direct MDA administration. Active duration extended.

metabolism.notes: Lysine amide bond hydrolysed to liberate MDA. Then MDA follows its own CYP2D6/2B6 metabolism.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Once MDA is liberated, same CYP2D6 considerations as MDA.

notes: Investigational prodrug being developed for delayed-onset, smoother PK profile suitable for psychotherapy contexts. WO2023028022A1 patent. Lykos and other developers are exploring this class. Category 'Antidepressant' in source is incorrect — this is an entactogen prodrug.

name: Mdai

binding.notes: Johnson, Frescas, Oberlender, Nichols 1991.
~12× selective for SERT over DAT — most SERT-selective of the entactogen class.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Conformationally constrained 2-aminoindane — the rigid indane ring locks the geometry that drives SERT selectivity. Acts predominantly as SERT-selective releaser/reuptake inhibitor with minimal DA effect. Nichols' original goal was a 'non-neurotoxic MDMA' — animal data shows much-reduced serotonergic terminal damage vs MDMA, but cases of fatal hyperthermia in users have been reported. Not as safe as the 'non-neurotoxic' label implies clinically.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Serotonin syndrome risk — multiple fatalities reported from MDAI + serotonergic combinations.

notes: Originally developed by David Nichols (Purdue) as a tool to study selective serotonin release without neurotoxicity. Sold as 'sparkle'/'mindy' RC in 2010s. Marketing as 'safe MDMA alternative' is misleading — Corkery review documents fatalities and the Pálenicek 2016 rat LD50 study shows narrow safety margin.

name: 5-apb

binding.notes: Iversen et al 2013.
Brandt et al 2020 — extremely potent releaser (3-10× more potent than MDA).
Full nM agonist at 5-HT2B — major cardiotoxicity concern. Same fenfluramine-class red flag.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Benzofuran replacement of methylenedioxy ring shifts pharmacology toward more balanced SNDR release (less SERT-selective than MDMA). Combined with potent 5-HT2B agonism, this drives the documented cardiotoxicity in fatal cases — fenfluramine-like proliferative effects on heart valves.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Serotonin syndrome — multiple fatalities documented in 5-APB users with concurrent serotonergic agents.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Serotonergic comedown; long-lasting because of extended half-life.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Potent full agonist at nM concentrations — substantial cardiac valvulopathy risk. Fenfluramine-class flag.

data_gaps_remaining: Human PK data — no published controlled-dose study
notes: Sold extensively as 'benzofury' 2010-2014; UK ban May 2014 followed multiple fatalities. The combination of low-nM SNDR release and potent 5-HT2B agonism makes it significantly more dangerous than MDMA at equivalent subjective doses.

name: 6-apb

binding.notes: Extremely potent DA releaser — single-digit nM. Drives stimulant character and abuse liability.
Even more potent at 5-HT2B than 5-APB. Significant cardiac valvulopathy risk.
Higher α2A affinity than 5-APB.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: More balanced SNDR profile than 5-APB but with shifted DAT/SERT ratio favouring DA release — more stimulant, more reinforcing. Combined with 5-HT2B agonism: cardiotoxic at exposures users seek.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Long serotonergic comedown reflecting extended half-life.

notes: 6-APB has longer onset (~2 h) and longer duration (8-12 h) than MDMA. Multiple fatalities in UK/EU 2012-2014.

name: 5-mapb

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-methyl version of 5-APB — analogous to MDMA/MDA relationship. Slightly longer half-life, more SERT-selective release than 5-APB. Inherits the 5-HT2B agonism / cardiotoxicity flag of the parent. Iversen 2013 data shows similar nanomolar 5-HT2B agonism.

off_targets.notes: Class inference, not a measurement: benzofurans as a class are 5-HT2B agonists (Rickli 2015), but this compound was not in that panel and no measured value for it was retrieved. Previously mis-cited to a 2012 editorial.

data_gaps_remaining: 5-HT2B specific data for the N-methyl variant
notes: N-methyl variant of 5-APB. Sold as RC. Inherits cardiotoxicity concerns.

name: 6-mapb

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-methyl variant of 6-APB. Same class-level mechanism. Brandt 2020 release data: S-6-MABB (the S-N-methyl-α-methyl variant) DAT EC50=41 nM, NET EC50=77 nM, SERT EC50=54 nM in rat synaptosomes — balanced SNDRA. 5-HT2B agonism inherited from 6-APB scaffold.

notes: N-methyl-6-APB. Limited direct pharmacology data; class-level extrapolation only.

name: 5-eapb

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-ethyl-5-APB. By analogy to MDE vs MDMA, N-ethyl substitution should reduce DA release relative to 5-HT release — i.e. less stimulant. Direct pharmacology data sparse.

notes: Research chemical, sparse peer-reviewed data. Pharmacology inferred from class.

name: 6-eapb

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-ethyl-6-APB. Same SAR reasoning as 5-EAPB. No direct human data.

notes: Research chemical with no direct pharmacology data.

name: 5-apdb

binding.notes: Very weak DAT — near-pure NE/5-HT releaser-inhibitor.
Lower potency at 5-HT2B than 5-APB but still partial agonism — lower but not zero cardiac risk.
Notably high 5-HT2C affinity — may contribute to subjective effects.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Saturated benzofuran (dihydrobenzofuran) ring. Lower DA release than 5-APB — more selectively serotonergic.

notes: Dihydrobenzofuran variant. More selective for serotonin than 5-APB.

name: 6-apdb

binding.notes: Potent 5-HT2B agonist (similar to 6-APB scaffold).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Like 5-APDB but with the benzofuran oxygen migrated to the 6-position. Higher 5-HT2B and lower DAT compared to 5-APDB.

notes: Dihydrobenzofuran variant. Closely related to 6-APB.

name: 5-mapdb

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-methyl-5-APDB — like other N-methyl substitutions in this class, slightly shifts the DAT/SERT balance.

notes: N-methyl dihydrobenzofuran variant.

name: 4,4-dmar

binding.notes: Citation removed: this value was attributed to doi:10.1016/j.neuropharm.2018.06.025, which is a pediatric traumatic-brain-injury therapy review. Verified against PubMed/Crossref in the 2026-08-01 topicality audit. The number is retained but is now unsourced — treat as unverified. Niello et al 2018 — single-digit nM SNDRA.

Verified against PubMed/Crossref in the 2026-08-01 topicality audit. The number is retained but is now unsourced — treat as unverified. Inhibits VMAT2 — like MDMA — supports neurotoxicity hypothesis.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Highly potent and well-balanced SNDRA — single-digit-nM at DAT, ~20 nM at SERT and NET. The aminorex parent (1960s anorectic) was withdrawn for pulmonary hypertension; the dimethyl analogues retain this risk profile plus add serotonergic toxicity. The serotonergic component (5-HT2B + massive 5-HT release) is the proposed mechanism of the >30 fatal serotonin-syndrome-like cases reported in Europe 2013-2014.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Lethal serotonin syndrome — multiple confirmed fatalities.

off_targets.notes: Citation removed: this value was attributed to doi:10.1016/j.neuropharm.2018.06.025, which is a pediatric traumatic-brain-injury therapy review. Verified against PubMed/Crossref in the 2026-08-01 topicality audit. The number is retained but is now unsourced — treat as unverified.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Parent aminorex causes pulmonary arterial hypertension (1960s clinical disaster).

notes: 31 fatalities in Europe 2013-2014 (19 in Northern Ireland alone). EU controlled 2015. The most dangerous compound in this list by user-fatality ratio. Schedule equivalent in most jurisdictions.

name: Methamnetamine

binding.notes: Wee/Negus dataset. Balanced SNDRA, low-nM.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Naphthyl ring replacement of phenyl gives a balanced SNDRA with very low nM potency. PAL-287 was investigated as a stimulant-use-disorder treatment because the 5-HT release dampens DA reinforcement. Methamnetamine is the N-methyl analogue.

metabolism.notes: Aromatic hydroxylation of the naphthalene ring is a major pathway in vitro.

notes: Triple-monoamine releaser with research-pharmacology pedigree (PAL series). No published human controlled data; very limited recreational user-base data.

name: Mexedrone

binding.notes: McLaughlin et al 2017 — only weak SERT releasing activity. Inactive as DAT/NET releaser.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: β-methoxy modification of mephedrone scaffold collapses transporter activity — only weak SERT release remains, with no DA/NE release. Subjective effects in users are weak compared to mephedrone, consistent with this. Sold as a 'legal' mephedrone replacement; actually weakly active.

notes: Sold 2015+ as legal mephedrone alternative. Pharmacology disappointing; actual recreational potency may reflect contamination with active congeners.

name: 5-iai

binding.notes: Halogenated aminoindane variant of MDAI — similar SERT-selective release profile. Iodo substituent is a classic 'safety' analogue used by Nichols to map non-neurotoxic releasers.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Conformationally constrained aminoindane similar to MDAI. SERT-selective releaser. Lower in-vivo serotonergic neurotoxicity than MDMA in animals.

notes: Halogenated MDAI relative. Originally a Nichols/Purdue research probe.

name: 5-apdi

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Indane-fused 2-aminopropyl variant. Sparse direct data; presumed SERT-preferring releaser by class analogy.

notes: Limited published pharmacology.

name: 5-it

binding.notes: Potent and selective MAO-A inhibitor — this is the dominant pharmacology and the source of its lethality. Not primarily a transporter substrate.
Triple monoamine releaser similar to AMT.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Positional isomer of α-methyltryptamine (AMT). Acts as both monoamine releaser AND potent MAO-A inhibitor — a chemically guaranteed serotonin syndrome generator at supratherapeutic doses. Self-MAO-inhibition prolongs its own half-life. The combination accounts for the cluster of fatalities reported when 5-IT entered EU markets 2011-2013.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Fatal in combination: four UK deaths reported with 5-IT at 0.4-1.2 mg/L femoral blood, three of them alongside other serotonergic drugs (MDMA, methylone, 6-APB, MDA, BZP) and attributed to the combined 'cocktail effect'.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Built-in MAO-A inhibition while releasing 5-HT — fatal interaction with own pharmacology and any other serotonergic input.

notes: One of the most dangerous compounds in this list. Entered EU market 2011 sold as legal MDMA replacement; clustered fatalities (Sweden 14, UK ≥6, others) led to rapid scheduling. Not an entactogen-class compound clinically — it is an MAOI+releaser. Mislabeled by retail.

name: 5-meo-amt

binding.notes: Induces head-twitch response in mice via 5-HT2A — a classic psychedelic assay readout. Very high 5-HT2A potency.
Weak MAO-A inhibitor.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Dominant pharmacology is 5-HT2A agonism (psychedelic) — the releaser activity is secondary. Shulgin TIHKAL dose 2.5-4.5 mg; duration 12-18 h. NOT an entactogen — this is misclassified.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Fatal serotonin syndrome — multiple deaths reported in 2003-2004 US cluster.

notes: MISCATEGORIZED: This is a serotonergic psychedelic (5-HT2A agonist), not an entactogen. Closely related to 5-MeO-DMT / AMT. Recategorize as Psychedelic. Schedule I in US.

name: MDOH

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-hydroxy variant of MDA. The N-OH is metabolically labile and rapidly reduced to MDA in vivo — MDOH effectively acts as a prodrug of MDA. PIHKAL #114; dose 100-160 mg, duration 3-6 h.

metabolism.notes: Rapid N-OH reduction to MDA in vivo. MDOH is functionally an MDA prodrug.

data_gaps_remaining: Direct binding/release data — only PIHKAL human dose-response is published
notes: PIHKAL #114. Functionally an MDA prodrug.

name: MDPR

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-propyl extension of MDA scaffold. Per Shulgin SAR — extension beyond N-ethyl progressively kills monoamine release activity at the human transporters. PIHKAL describes weak activity at ~200 mg.

notes: PIHKAL compound. N-propyl chain reduces potency. Limited published pharmacology.

name: MDAL

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-allyl-MDA. PIHKAL compound with sparse direct pharmacology data.

notes: PIHKAL N-allyl variant.

name: 3,4-Methylenedioxyamphetamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: DUPLICATE of MDA — see MDA record for full data.

notes: DUPLICATE: Same compound as 'MDA' in this list. Recommend deduplication.

name: MMDA

binding.notes: Shulgin PIHKAL #132 — described as 'psychedelic with euphoric properties.' 5-HT2A agonism is the dominant pharmacology, more than transporter substrate activity. Active dose 100-250 mg, duration 6-8 h.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Methoxy substitution on the methylenedioxyamphetamine ring shifts pharmacology from entactogen toward psychedelic — more 5-HT2A agonism, less monoamine release. MMDA is the proposed active metabolite of myristicin (nutmeg).

notes: PIHKAL #132. Proposed active metabolite of myristicin from nutmeg.

name: MMDA-2

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: PIHKAL #133. Methoxy position isomer of MMDA. Psychedelic > entactogen.

notes: PIHKAL #133. Positional methoxy isomer of MMDA.

name: MMDA-3a

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: PIHKAL #134. Sparse data.

notes: PIHKAL positional isomer with negligible published data.

name: MMDA-3b

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: PIHKAL positional isomer. No direct pharmacology data.

notes: PIHKAL.

name: DMMDA

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: PIHKAL #62. Di-methoxy version of MMDA — pushed further toward psychedelic/2C-x-like profile. Shulgin reported active at 30-75 mg.

notes: PIHKAL #62.

name: DMMDA-2

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: PIHKAL #63. Positional isomer of DMMDA. Sparse data.

notes: PIHKAL #63.

name: 2-BR-4,5-MDA

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Ortho-bromo MDA — by 2C-B/DOB analogy, 6-bromo substitution markedly increases 5-HT2A binding affinity. Likely shifts pharmacology toward psychedelic. PIHKAL.

notes: PIHKAL halogenated MDA.

name: 2-Bromo-4,5-MDMA

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-methyl variant of 2-Br-MDA. Same 5-HT2A-affinity-boosting bromine effect.

notes: Halogenated MDMA analogue. Negligible published data.

name: 2T-MMDA-3a

binding.notes: Weak MAO inhibitor — lacks basic nitrogen typical of MAOIs, so the activity is mild. Probably contributes to nutmeg's monoaminergic effects.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Itself an aromatic ether with no primary amine — not a classical entactogen. Hypothesised to be metabolised in humans to MMDA (3-methoxy-4,5-MDA) via an aminotransferase/CYP-mediated process that adds an amine to the allyl side chain — this proposed amphetamine metabolite would then act on 5-HT2A. The metabolic conversion has been demonstrated in rodent in vitro systems but the in vivo human conversion is debated and quantitatively small. Nutmeg's psychoactivity probably stems from a combination of weak MAO inhibition, slow generation of trace amphetamine metabolites, and CNS effects of other constituents (elemicin, safrole).

routes.notes: Onset of nutmeg intoxication 3-8 hours; duration 24-48 h. Pharmacokinetics dominated by extensive first-pass metabolism.

metabolism.notes: Aminotransferase-mediated formation of 3-methoxy-4,5-MDA in rodents. Quantitative role in humans unclear.

notes: Nutmeg primary aromatic ether. Not a true entactogen — included in this group because of the methylenedioxy ring. Psychoactivity is delayed (3-8 h onset) and dysphoric/deliriant rather than empathogenic.

shared_mechanism: Substrate-type monoamine releasers at SERT, NET, and DAT. Compound enters the neuron via the same transporter it will then reverse — once inside, it triggers efflux of stored monoamines, with VMAT2 inhibition contributing to cytosolic monoamine availability. The 3,4-methylenedioxy ring is the entactogen signature: it shifts SERT selectivity above DAT (the opposite of methamphetamine). The α-methyl group protects against MAO oxidation, doubling duration vs the deaminated phenethylamines. The N-substituent modulates the DAT:SERT release ratio: N-H (MDA) gives broad release with some 5-HT2A agonism; N-methyl (MDMA) is the prototypical entactogen with strong SERT/NET, modest DAT; N-ethyl (MDE) collapses DA release; N-propyl/N-allyl further reduce all activity. Ring substitution (e.g., 5-methoxy → MMDA, 6-bromo → 2-Br-MDA) shifts pharmacology from releaser toward direct 5-HT2A agonist psychedelic. The class is also defined by potent 5-HT2B agonism (MDA Ki ≈100 nM, MDMA ≈500 nM), responsible for the cardiac valvular fibrosis risk shared by all members at heavy chronic exposure.
shared_pk_summary: Oral bioavailability ~70%, Tmax 1.5-2.5 h, half-life 6-10 h for the prototypical MDxx compounds. Metabolism is primarily CYP2D6 (O-demethylenation of the catechol — generating reactive ortho-quinones that mechanism-based-inhibit the enzyme) and CYP2B6 (N-dealkylation). The mechanism-based inhibition of CYP2D6 is the source of MDMA's characteristic nonlinear PK: doubling the dose more than doubles AUC, half-life lengthens at higher doses, and the inhibited CYP2D6 takes ~10 days to recover via de novo protein synthesis. This means CYP2D6 polymorphism has less impact than predicted from first principles, but co-administration of other CYP2D6 substrates is dangerous — repeat-dosing within a week stacks exposure unpredictably regardless of genotype. Major active metabolites are MDA from MDMA (N-demethylation, half-life ~12 h — explains next-day stimulant tail). HMMA via COMT methylation of HHMA is the major urinary metabolite. Phase II glucuronide/sulfate conjugation of HMMA dominates elimination.
shared_safety: Acute: serotonin syndrome (with any MAOI / serotonergic agent — absolute contraindication for MAOIs); SIADH-mediated hyponatremia (especially with the polydipsia typical of recreational use; women at higher risk); hyperthermia driven by NE release + skeletal muscle activity + impaired heat dissipation, capable of causing rhabdomyolysis, DIC, multi-organ failure. Cardiovascular: dose-dependent HR and BP increases. Chronic: 5-HT2B-mediated cardiac valvular fibrosis (fenfluramine-class concern); serotonergic axonal pruning at heavy repeated doses (animal evidence robust; human imaging with [11C]-DASB PET shows reduced SERT availability in heavy users with partial recovery on abstinence). Lifetime exposure matters more than single-dose intensity for valve disease and SERT downregulation. Re-dosing within a session is particularly inefficient and increases risk because CYP2D6 is already inhibited and 5-HT pools are depleted — gives more side effects without more euphoria.
sar_summary: α-methyl: protects from MAO oxidation, doubles duration relative to phenethylamine. N-substituent: H = MDA (broad release + 5-HT2A agonist character); methyl = MDMA (canonical entactogen, balanced SERT/NET, weaker DA); ethyl = MDE (collapses DA, pure entactogen); larger N-alkyls progressively kill activity. Ring substitution: 3,4-methylenedioxy = entactogen signature (SERT-selective); halogenation (Br, I) on the ring increases 5-HT2A binding (psychedelic shift); methoxy substitution (e.g., MMDA) increases 5-HT2A agonism at the cost of release; benzofuran ring-replacement (5-APB/6-APB) gives single-digit-nM SNDRA potency with high 5-HT2B agonism (more dangerous); 2-aminoindane scaffold (MDAI) constrains geometry for SERT-selectivity (less neurotoxic per Nichols' design but still capable of fatal hyperthermia). β-keto (cathinone) ring shifts toward stimulant character with VMAT2 inactivity (methylone is 4-5× less potent at SERT release than MDMA). Lysine-amide prodrugs (Lys-MDA, Lys-MDMA) extend onset/duration with no intrinsic activity until peptidase cleavage.

shared_mechanism: The benzofuran ring (and its saturated dihydrobenzofuran analogue) replaces the methylenedioxy of MDxx with a furan oxygen, while keeping the α-methyl phenethylamine pharmacophore. The substitution dramatically increases potency at human monoamine transporters: 5-APB and 6-APB are 3-10× more potent than MDA at every transporter (single-digit nM EC50 at rat DAT/NET/SERT). The class-defining liability is potent agonism at 5-HT2B (5-APB EC50 280 nM Emax 61%, 6-APB EC50 140 nM Emax 70% — both full agonists in the nanomolar range), which substantially exceeds MDMA's 5-HT2B affinity. This explains the higher rate of fatal cardiac events seen with APB-class drugs at recreational doses. The 5- and 6-positional isomers differ: 5-APB is more SERT-selective; 6-APB is more potent at DAT. Dihydrobenzofuran (APDB) variants have weaker DAT activity and shift toward NRI/SSRA profile. N-methyl substitution (MAPB) gives MDMA-like profile shifts (less DAT release). N-ethyl (EAPB) collapses DA release further.
shared_pk_summary: Longer half-lives than MDMA (8-12 h reported for APBs vs 6-8 h MDMA). Slower onset (~2 h vs ~1 h for MDMA). Hepatic metabolism via CYP2D6 (analogous to MDMA) plus likely furan ring oxidation (epoxide intermediates — potential hepatotoxic mechanism not well-characterised). No controlled human PK studies published.
shared_safety: Acute: same serotonin syndrome risks as MDMA but multiplied by higher transporter potency. Multiple fatalities documented in UK 2012-2014 ('benzofury'), prompting UK ban. The potent 5-HT2B agonism makes chronic use highly likely to cause cardiac valvular fibrosis (fenfluramine-class concern, but more potent than fenfluramine on a molar basis). Furan ring metabolism may generate reactive epoxides — hepatotoxicity signal in case reports. Long duration combined with vasoconstriction makes hyperthermia/cardiotoxicity worse than equivalent MDMA dose.
sar_summary: Furan O position (5 vs 6) determines DAT:SERT ratio. Dihydro- (saturated) form weakens DAT. Same N-substitution effects as MDxx family: H = APB (SNDRA), methyl = MAPB, ethyl = EAPB. All retain potent 5-HT2B agonism — there is no published structural modification that decouples desirable release activity from this cardiotoxic off-target in this scaffold.

shared_mechanism: The 2-aminoindane scaffold conformationally constrains the phenethylamine into a rigid 'extended' geometry. This geometry is favourable for SERT activity but disfavours DAT — yielding selective serotonin releasers/reuptake inhibitors with minimal dopamine effect. MDAI (5,6-methylenedioxy-2-aminoindane) is the prototype, developed by David Nichols at Purdue as a 'non-neurotoxic MDMA' research tool. SERT IC50 512 nM, DAT IC50 5920 nM (~12-fold SERT-selective) in rat synaptosomes (Johnson et al 1991). The reduced neurotoxicity in animals stems from low DA-mediated oxidative stress; serotonergic axonal pruning is still possible but markedly reduced.
shared_pk_summary: Limited published human PK. Onset 1-2 h, duration 4-6 h reported by users. Hepatic metabolism with CYP2D6 contribution presumed.
shared_safety: The 'non-neurotoxic' label has been misleading in practice — Corkery 2013 documented fatalities, and Pálenicek 2016 rat LD50 work demonstrated a narrow safety margin with severe hyperthermia. SERT-selective release still produces serotonin syndrome with MAOIs and SSRIs. 5-HT2B agonism — likely retained by class — adds cardiac concern.
sar_summary: Aminoindane core (2-aminopropyl built into a cyclopentane ring fused to benzene) gives rigidity. 5,6-methylenedioxy = MDAI; 5-iodo = 5-IAI (similar profile, halogenated); 5-amino (unsubstituted) = 5-APDI = IAP. Without ring substitution, the parent 2-aminoindane is itself a selective NRI used as a research reference. N-methylation reduces serotonergic potency.

shared_mechanism: 2-amino-oxazoline ring system. Parent aminorex was a 1960s anorectic (withdrawn for pulmonary arterial hypertension). The dimethyl/methyl analogues retain release activity at all three monoamine transporters; 4,4'-DMAR is a single-digit-nM SNDRA (DAT EC50 8.6 nM, SERT 18.5 nM, NET 26.9 nM) and a VMAT2 inhibitor.
shared_safety: The most dangerous compounds in the entactogen/empathogen-adjacent space by user-fatality ratio. 4,4'-DMAR caused >30 fatal cases in EU 2013-2014 (cluster in Northern Ireland alone: 19 deaths). Mechanism: serotonin syndrome from massive 5-HT release, plus retained aminorex pulmonary toxicity, plus VMAT2-mediated neurotoxicity. Avoid entirely.
sar_summary: Methylation at the 4-position of the oxazoline (cis-4-methyl) and on the phenyl ring (4'-methyl) gives 4,4'-DMAR — the most active and most fatal variant. 3,4-DMAR (3'-methyl instead of 4'-methyl) is somewhat less potent.

shared_mechanism: α-methyl tryptamines combine 5-HT2A agonism (psychedelic) with monoamine releaser activity AND MAO-A inhibition. The MAO-A inhibition is the dangerous feature: it is built into the compound's own pharmacology, so the released 5-HT cannot be metabolised. 5-IT (5-API, the indole positional isomer of AMT) is a particularly potent MAO-A inhibitor. 5-MeO-AMT adds 5-methoxy substitution that boosts 5-HT2A agonism markedly — Shulgin's α,O-DMS — extremely potent at 2.5-5 mg active dose.
shared_pk_summary: Very long duration (12-18 h for 5-MeO-AMT) reflecting MAO inhibition prolonging the compound's own half-life.
shared_safety: Built-in pharmacological foot-gun. The MAO-A inhibition guarantees fatal serotonin syndrome with any additional serotonergic input. Multiple fatality clusters: 5-MeO-AMT in US 2003-2004, 5-IT in EU 2011-2013 (>20 confirmed deaths). MISCATEGORIZED in this group: these are tryptamine psychedelics, not entactogens.
sar_summary: Adding 5-methoxy boosts 5-HT2A. Moving the 2-aminopropyl from indole-3 (true tryptamines) to indole-5 (5-IT/5-API) shifts activity from receptor agonism to MAO inhibition.

shared_mechanism: β-keto (cathinone) shifts the amphetamine scaffold toward stimulant character. Methylone (3,4-methylenedioxymethcathinone) is the β-keto MDMA — much weaker SERT release (~5× less than MDMA) but retains stimulant-like DAT activity, no VMAT2 inhibition (lower neurotoxicity). Mephedrone and 4-MEC inherit similar profiles. The cathinone class is generally less SERT-selective than the MDxx amphetamines, more reinforcing, and shorter-acting. β-methoxy modifications (mexedrone) collapse activity.
shared_pk_summary: Shorter half-lives than MDxx (mephedrone ~2-3 h). Hepatic metabolism via CYP2D6 (analogous demethylenation). Cathinones generally have lower oral bioavailability than amphetamines.
shared_safety: Lower serotonergic neurotoxicity than MDMA at equivalent doses but higher abuse potential due to DAT activity. Cardiotoxicity from sympathomimetic load. Methylone cleared US Phase 1 trials for PTSD — apparently safer subjective profile than MDMA at equivalent serotonergic effect.
sar_summary: β-keto = stimulant shift, VMAT2-inactive. N-methyl vs N-ethyl: same dose-shifting as MDxx. Ring substitution: 3,4-methylenedioxy = methylone/butylone family; 4-methyl = mephedrone.

shared_mechanism: Naphthalene ring replacement of phenyl. PAL-287 (naphthylaminopropane) is a balanced SNDRA with single-digit-nM potency at all three monoamine transporters (5-HT 3.4 nM, NE 11.1 nM, DA 12.6 nM) — originally developed as a candidate stimulant-use-disorder treatment because the balanced release dampens DA reinforcement. Methamnetamine is the N-methyl analogue (similar profile).
shared_safety: Serotonin syndrome with MAOIs. No published fatalities cluster, but research-chemical exposure is low.
sar_summary: Naphthyl ring boosts potency at all transporters. N-methylation and N-ethylation shift the DAT:SERT ratio analogously to phenethylamine families.

class_name: Pyrovalerone cathinones (MDPV / α-PVP / MD-PHP family) — included by accident
shared_mechanism: Pure DAT/NET reuptake inhibitors with NO serotonergic activity. Pyrrolidine-N + extended α-alkyl chain. MDPV is the prototype; α-PVP, MD-PHP, MD-PiHP, α-PiHP all share the same NDRI profile. These are pure stimulants — not entactogens. Their inclusion in this group is a categorisation error.
shared_pk_summary: Hepatic CYP2D6/CYP1A2 metabolism. Short half-lives (2-4 h for MDPV).
shared_safety: High abuse potential, cardiovascular toxicity, agitation/psychosis (the 'bath salts' presentation). No serotonin syndrome risk because no serotonergic activity. Should be reclassified to a stimulant group.
sar_summary: Pyrrolidine N + α-alkyl chain length (propyl/butyl/pentyl/hexyl) tunes DAT potency. β-keto retained. Methylenedioxy ring on phenyl gives MD-PHP/MD-PiHP/MDPV.

class_name: Classical tryptamine psychedelics — miscategorized in this group
shared_mechanism: 5-HT2A agonists. Psilocin (active form of psilocybin), Ayahuasca (DMT + β-carboline MAOIs), Yopo (bufotenin/DMT snuff) all share 5-HT2A-driven psychedelic mechanism. NOT entactogens — they do not release monoamines significantly.
shared_safety: Class-typical psychedelic risks (HPPD, psychiatric exacerbation), with MAOI-specific risks for Ayahuasca.

shared_mechanism: Direct 5-HT2A agonists, not monoamine releasers. NBOMe N-substitution converts 2C-x parents into hyper-potent (sub-nM) 5-HT2A agonists with serious fatality risk.
shared_safety: NBOMe vasoconstriction, hyperthermia, seizures; multiple documented fatalities.

shared_mechanism: 5-HT1A, 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C agonism plus weak SERT inhibition. Fenfluramine-like serotonergic profile. Not strictly entactogens — produce dysphoric serotonergic effects more than empathy.
shared_safety: Headache, nausea, anxiety. mCPP is the active metabolite of trazodone.

shared_mechanism: CB1/CB2 receptor agonists. JWH-367 is a Huffman pyrrole cannabinoid. Has nothing in common with MDMA/entactogens — appears in this group by error.
